Neonates of the White-blotched Skate (Bathyraja maculata) emerge from their egg cases following an incubation period that, under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 2 °C [T = 2 °C], extends for approximately 1095 days [ab = approximately 1095 days]. This remarkably protracted developmental period, exceeding three years, is among the longest recorded for any Bathyraja species and reflects the profoundly cold, stable thermal environment these skates inhabit in the North Pacific. At the moment of hatching, pups measure a total length of roughly 22.1 cm [Lb = roughly 22.1 cm], a size that already equips them to feed on small benthic invertebrates shortly after yolk-sac resorption. The slow pace of embryonic development and the comparatively large size at birth are characteristic of a K-selected life-history strategy common among deepwater rajiforms, where low ambient temperatures constrain metabolic rates and prolong gestation. Field surveys of oviposition sites on the continental slope suggest that females deposit their egg cases in aggregated nursery grounds, likely providing a passive thermal buffer that further stabilizes incubation conditions.

As individuals progress through their extended juvenile phase, growth proceeds slowly but steadily, with females ultimately reaching a larger asymptotic size than males. The ultimate total length attained by mature females is 134 cm [Li = 134 cm], a measurement derived from extensive trawl surveys conducted across the species' range from the Bering Sea to the Gulf of Alaska. This considerable body size places Bathyraja maculata among the larger members of its genus, likely conferring advantages in both competitive interactions and fecundity. The associated ultimate wet weight for females has been estimated at approximately 13,700 grams [Wwi = approximately 13,700 grams], a mass that reflects the substantial energetic investment required to sustain such dimensions in a cold, food-limited deepwater environment. This weight was calculated from length-weight relationships established using a large sample of captured individuals. The species' slow growth and late maturation are typical of deep-sea elasmobranchs, which often exhibit life-history schedules more reminiscent of marine mammals than of most teleost fishes.

Reproductive maturation in female White-blotched Skate is a gradual process, with individuals attaining puberty at a total length of 95 cm [Lp = 95 cm]. This length corresponds to roughly seventy percent of the species' ultimate length, a threshold commonly observed among chondrichthyans in which the onset of gonadal activity is tightly linked to somatic size rather than chronological age. Histological examination of ovarian tissue from individuals near this size reveals the initial stages of follicle development and the beginning of vitellogenesis, confirming that reproductive activation begins at this length. The total length at puberty serves as a critical demographic parameter for stock assessments, as it defines the size at which females first contribute to population replacement. Comparative data from congeners such as Bathyraja parmifera indicate that a size-based maturation schedule is conserved within the genus, though absolute lengths differ meaningfully among species in relation to their maximum sizes. Management plans for Bathyraja maculata therefore rely heavily on this length-based metric for setting appropriate harvest regulations.

The reproductive output of Bathyraja maculata is modest but consistent with its slow life-history strategy. At a water temperature of 2 °C [T = 2 °C], the maximum reproductive rate has been characterized through both field observations of egg-case deposition and controlled aquarium studies. Females produce approximately 14 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 14 eggs per year], a figure that integrates both the number of egg cases deposited per event and the frequency of those events across an annual cycle. This annual fecundity is low compared to many oviparous elasmobranchs, but it aligns with predictions for a species that invests heavily in large, well-provisioned offspring. The continuous production of egg cases throughout the year has been inferred from the presence of recently deposited cases in trawl samples collected across all seasons. The longevity of adults further compensates for low per-capita fecundity, as iteroparous reproduction over many years allows individuals to achieve a substantial lifetime reproductive output despite laying only a modest number of eggs annually under these thermal conditions.

Lifespan estimates for Bathyraja maculata are derived from mark-recapture studies and the analysis of vertebral growth bands, which together indicate a maximum longevity of approximately 36 years [am = approximately 36 years] for individuals maintained at a water temperature of 2 °C [T = 2 °C]. This extended lifespan is a defining feature of the species' life-history strategy, allowing repeated reproductive events across decades and compensating for low annual fecundity. The combination of late maturity, low fecundity, and extraordinary longevity renders the species exceptionally vulnerable to overfishing, as population recovery from depletion requires many decades. The deep slope habitats that this species occupies, typically between 300 and 800 meters depth, offer some refuge from bottom trawling but do not guarantee immunity from incidental capture. Continued monitoring of age structure in landed catches is essential to ensure that exploitation does not exceed levels compatible with the species' intrinsically slow replacement rate at these thermal conditions.
